headline_marked: [[11-party alliance begins long march]] from Dhaka to Chattogram today, pressuring govt on key demands
headline: 11-party alliance begins long march from Dhaka to Chattogram today, pressuring govt on key demands
summary: The Jamaat-e-Islami-led alliance aims to push for the implementation of a referendum verdict, resolve crises in fuel, power, and commodity prices, and seek justice for past crimes.
details: The Jamaat-e-Islami-led 11-party alliance has commenced a long march today, extending from Dhaka to Chattogram. This major event aims to intensify pressure on the government regarding several key demands.

The alliance's primary demands include the implementation of a referendum verdict, addressing the ongoing crises in fuel, power, and commodity prices, and ensuring justice for various crimes committed during the Awami League regime.

Jamaat Ameer and Opposition Leader Shafiqur Rahman, alongside other top leaders from the 11 constituent parties, are participating in the program. This long march is a significant part of the alliance's broader agitation strategy.

This long march follows approximately six and a half months after the BNP government took office on February 17. The alliance has maintained a consistent schedule of street agitations, including divisional rallies and sit-ins, almost monthly since April.

The current march is the first of four planned divisional long marches, with subsequent events scheduled from Dhaka to Rangpur, Khulna, and Sylhet in September and October. These will culminate in a grand rally in Dhaka on November 14.

Mia Golam Porwar, secretary general of Jamaat and convener of the long march committee, urged the government not to obstruct the event. He emphasized the opposition's constitutional and responsible role, asserting the march would be peaceful and lawful.

Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee criticized the opposition's timing, stating that six months is insufficient to complete all development work. He suggested the opposition should understand the scope of ongoing projects.

The long march began with an inaugural rally at Dhaka's Shapla Chattar. Subsequent rallies are planned at Chittagong Road in Narayanganj, Paduar Bazar and Chauddagram in Cumilla, Mahipal in Feni, and Mirsharai in Chattogram, concluding at Laldighi Maidan.
The alliance anticipates approximately 1,500 vehicles will participate in the long march, demonstrating the scale of their organized protest.

headline: Bangladesh sees highest dengue infection in 3 years, mixed serotypes increase risk
summary: Bangladesh is experiencing its highest dengue infection rate in three years, with a significant rise in cases and deaths since July. The co-circulation of two dengue serotypes, DEN-2 and DEN-3, is contributing to the rapid spread and increased risk.
details: Khalida Akter struggled to find a hospital bed for her 22-year-old son, Fatemi, who is suffering from dengue, after being turned away from two government hospitals. Private hospitals also face bed shortages, forcing families to consider expensive cabins.

The country is witnessing a sharp rise in dengue cases and deaths. Infections tripled from May to June, and again from June to July, with deaths also increasing threefold. August saw more than double the infections compared to the previous month.

This year, the DEN-3 serotype of the dengue virus has become predominant, but DEN-2 is also spreading significantly. The Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR) describes this as a 'mixed picture,' with public health experts suggesting that the co-circulation of two serotypes may contribute to the rapid transmission.

According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), over 40,000 patients have been hospitalized with dengue from January 1 to September 4 this year. This marks the highest number of admissions during the same period in the last three years, with 111 deaths recorded.

Public health experts and entomologists warn that dengue could become uncontrolled this month, potentially leading to a situation similar to 2023. The bed shortage is not limited to Dhaka but is also prevalent in other parts of the country where mosquito control and dengue treatment are inadequate.

Professor Halimur Rashid, Director of the Disease Control Branch of the Health Directorate, stated that controlling infection is not their responsibility. He added that government hospitals always have fewer beds than patients, and there are no deficiencies in treatment.

Bangladesh has experienced major dengue outbreaks since 2000, with infections exceeding 100,000 for the first time in 2019. However, 2023 broke all previous records, with 321,179 hospitalizations and 1,705 deaths.

The World Health Organization (WHO) notes that while infection with one serotype provides long-term immunity against it, protection against other serotypes is temporary. Subsequent infections with a different serotype can increase the risk of severe dengue, though no single serotype is inherently more dangerous.

IEDCR Director Dr. Kazi Ahmed Zaki reported that a survey in June across Bandarban, Barguna, and Patuakhali districts showed DEN-3 as predominant in urban areas of Barguna and Patuakhali, while DEN-2 was more common in rural areas and Bandarban. This indicates a complex, mixed serotype situation.
